note: Confirmation/status signals read back from a drive or final control element about its own state — an X-prefix code (see Signal Origin Prefix below) marks a signal as coming FROM the field, distinct from a command going TO it. The numbered codes XB01, XB02 etc. below are this category’s specific, standardized meanings.
This is the DI (digital/binary input) category in KKS terms — conditioned by binary signal conditioning modules, e.g. a limit/level switch’s raw contact wired straight into the system.

meaning: Binary limit signals derived from analog process signals
note: Also a binary (DI-type) signal, but computed rather than wired directly — e.g. a high/low alarm derived from a 4-20mA transmitter’s reading, not a dedicated physical switch.
e.g. black-box or dedicated, packaged I&C not otherwise covered.
Signals not assigned to a specific control system, e.g. control interface tiles.

meaning: Higher-level static individual and group alarm signals
note: e.g. power supply failure, fuse status — persistent fault conditions.

This is the AI (analog input) category in KKS terms — a continuous measured value (e.g. a live 4-20mA reading) rather than a binary state. Unlike XB’s command/feedback codes, an analog value has no fixed per-number "meaning" table to look up — the number just identifies which analog point on the device it is.

meaning: Higher-level dynamic individual and group alarm signals
note: Transient/momentary alarm conditions, as distinct from XM's static ones.
Protective logic, alarm logic, etc.

Used in the "Signal Code" scheme (feedback/status signals FROM the field) — a signal taken straight from its source, e.g. directly from a switch contact. See the Application Code (Y) entry below for the separate scheme used for commands.

Used in the "Signal Code" scheme (feedback/status signals FROM the field) — a signal that has passed through logic, e.g. the output of an AND gate. Distinguishes a raw input from a processed/interlocked one carrying the same category letter.

A feedback/acknowledgment signal read back FROM the drive confirming it is actually on/open — not the command sent TO it. The corresponding command uses a separate KKS suffix scheme, the "Application Code" (Y-prefix, e.g. YB01) — confirmed in Siemens TXP-CLC training documentation, and listed further down this page. XB, as a Signal Code (X-prefix), specifically identifies a signal coming back from the field.
The corresponding "closed/off confirmed" feedback read back from the drive, paired with XB01 the same way — not a command.
e.g. raise frequency/voltage/setpoint.
Generator/pump-turbine unit running in generating mode.
Running in pumping mode (pumped-storage units).
Field control level, local.
Field control level, remote.

The complementary "off-state confirmed" feedback paired with XB01 for the same drive — a real drive typically wires BOTH XB01 and XB51 so the control system can distinguish a genuine OFF state from a stuck or failed-to-report contact, rather than inferring OFF purely from the absence of the XB01 ON feedback.
The complementary feedback paired with XB02.
A raw NO-contact signal, e.g. from a level or limit switch — distinct from XH, which is a limit derived from an analog transmitter rather than a dedicated switch.
e.g. a valve caught mid-travel, neither confirmed open nor closed.
A fault/disturbance condition on this signal.

category: XH — Binary Limits Derived From Analog Signals
note: A high-limit alarm computed from a continuous analog transmitter's reading (e.g. 4-20mA), not a dedicated physical switch — the functional counterpart to XG for signals with an analog source instead of a switch.

The command mirror of the confirmed feedback code XB01: this is the instruction sent TO the drive to turn on/open, as distinct from XB01, the confirmation read back FROM it that it has done so.
The command mirror of the confirmed feedback code XB02.

The specific example given in Siemens TXP-CLC training documentation for a real device (MBV41AA001) — the source does not spell out what function 22 represents, so it’s listed here as the directly-sourced reference point for the numbering range, not a decoded meaning.

The complete, officially-sourced counterpart list to the X (Signal Origins) table above, from the same McGraw-Hill KKS appendix (Siemens 1995 source booklet): YA, YB, YC, YJ, YL, YN, YP, YQ, YT, YV, YW. Notably shorter than the X list -- there is no YG, YH, YK, YM, YS, or YU, because a binary process signal, a derived limit, a protection trip, a static/dynamic alarm, or a turbine speed reading are inherently things the system reads, not things it commands.

The command-side counterpart to XB, confirmed in both the McGraw-Hill KKS appendix and Siemens TXP-CLC training documentation: an output sent TO a drive or final control element, as opposed to XB’s status read back FROM it. This is the category to use for a DO (digital/binary output) in KKS terms -- there is no separate YG for that, since Control Interface already covers on/off, open/close-type commands.

This is the AO (analog output) category in KKS terms -- the command-side counterpart to XQ (AI). A continuous outgoing value, e.g. a 4-20mA setpoint sent to a control valve positioner or a VFD speed reference, as opposed to XQ’s continuous incoming reading.
